source: Shen, Druckmann and Zou (2026) Unlocking LLM creativity in science through analogical reasoning
finding: Closest test so far of an explicit 'find the shared relational structure first, then search' step. Analogical reasoning (AR) extracts the problem's relational structure, picks far domains, then searches for solutions. It beat a cross-domain baseline and a no-domain baseline on diversity and novelty. This is a structure-first step for solutions, not for blends, so it supports gap 1 only by analogy.
numbers: 50 research problems, 150 generations per problem per setting, 3 LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Flash), temperature 1.0. Solution Vendi diversity +90-173% and domain Vendi +100-115% over the next best baseline. Share of novel solutions: Claude 1.6% (no-domain), 21.6% (cross-domain), 50.4% (AR); Gemini 8.9, 37.8, 68.9. Baselines collapse: only about 5% of generated domains unique, 57-66% of solutions unique. LLM calls per generation: AR 2, cross-domain 2, no-domain 1.
quote: AR generates analogies to cross-domain problems based on shared relational structure, then uses those analogies to search for novel solutions.
limits: Novelty and diversity judged by LLMs (human check: AR more novel 78% of the time, kappa .445, 50 pairs). Cost matched only against the cross-domain arm (2 calls each). Tasks are biomedical research problems, not noun-noun blends. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A 2-call 'extract structure, then search' step is a cheap way to raise novelty at near-equal cost. The direct blend-validity test of a generic-space step is still missing.

source: Shen, Druckmann and Zou (2026) analogical reasoning: domain distance and downstream case studies
finding: Distance and downstream result. AR analogies came from domains much further from the problem than baselines, and the resulting solutions were implemented by a coding agent on four biomedical tasks with gains against published baselines. First downstream test of far-seed solutions found, but there is no near-seed arm, so best distance is not answered.
numbers: Domain Distance (LLM-judged, 0-10): AR 6.99 / 6.83 / 7.53 (Claude/GPT/Gemini) vs no-domain 2.29 / 3.08 / 3.37; order no-domain < cross-domain < ground-truth < AR. Analogy novelty 4.82 / 5.27 / 5.58. Structural depth about equal across arms (7.06-8.60). Downstream: about 13-fold gain on a distributional metric for perturbation prediction, best AUPRC on cell-cell communication, Spearman .729 for brain-region interactions, state of the art on 2 oligonucleotide datasets. Human-LLM agreement on distance 88.6%, on novelty 75.7%.
limits: One solution implemented per problem (4 cases), no replication, no near-distance arm, no equal-effort baseline implemented. Implementation by a coding agent adds noise. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Supports 'far seeds raise novelty and can pay off downstream', but the best distance is untested.

source: Deng, Brucks and Toubia (2026) Examining and addressing barriers to diversity in LLM-generated ideas
finding: Idea diversity of GPT-4o is limited by two things: fixation inside one session and no 'knowledge partitioning' across samples. Ordinary personas (varied backgrounds) fix the second; chain-of-thought fixes the first; together they beat humans. Higher temperature barely helped. Cross-sample variety comes from varied cues, so randomised seed pairs plus a structured step are the plausible route for blends.
numbers: GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-11-20), N=99 simulated participants per arm, 10 ideas each (brainstorm task). Unique category combinations: human 206, LLM default 88, LLM ordinary persona 210, LLM creative-entrepreneur persona 164 (Table 2). With 83 per arm: human 197, human CoT 193, LLM CoT 152, LLM persona+CoT 248 (26% above humans); categories 27-28 in all arms. Within one person: human 12.68 vs LLM 12.46 categories (no gap). First-idea pairwise distance 2.41 human vs 1.51 LLM (p<.001). Temperature 1.5 gave a marginal gain; 2.0 gave garbled text.
limits: One model, one task, GPT-4o labels the categories. Persona+CoT uses more tokens than the default arm; no token matching. Not a blend task.
agent_relevance: Varied cues (personas or seed pairs) are the lever for set-level diversity; raising temperature is not.

source: Meincke, Mollick and Terwiesch (2024) Prompting diverse ideas: increasing AI idea variance
finding: 35 prompt variants for GPT-4 idea generation. Chain-of-thought gave the most diverse pool, near human groups. Persona prompts gave small gains. Pooling many sessions of mixed prompts (hybrid) was among the least diverse.
numbers: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of the idea pool (lower = more diverse): group of students 0.243; CoT 0.255; base prompt 0.386 (abstract quotes 0.377); Steve Jobs 0.371; creative entrepreneur 0.348; hybrid brainstorming (40 sessions pooled) 0.428. Unique ideas reachable: about 3,700 (base) to 4,700 (CoT). 100 ideas per session, 10 sessions per arm.
limits: One model (GPT-4), one product task, embedding similarity as the diversity proxy. Working paper. Equal idea counts but CoT uses extra tokens.
agent_relevance: Pooling many same-model samples does not fix homogeneity; a structured generate-then-revise step does.

source: Wenger and Kenett (2025) We're different, we're the same: creative homogeneity across LLMs
finding: Across 22 LLMs from many families, answers to standard creativity tests (AUT, FF, DAT) are far more alike than human answers, though individual LLM originality matches or beats humans. Creative system prompts raised originality but left variability well below humans.
numbers: AUT variability (mean cosine distance between respondents, higher = more diverse): humans 0.738; LLMs baseline prompt 0.459; 'more creative' 0.503; 'very creative' (with $200 reward text) 0.576; 'not creative' 0.492. Individual originality: humans 0.695, baseline LLM 0.711, very creative 0.754. Tests run on one model per family (7 models) to avoid family effects.
limits: Short-answer tests, embedding scoring (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), Prolific humans. No seed-based blending.
agent_relevance: Role prompting is a weak lever against cross-model sameness; do not rely on it alone.

source: Jiang et al. (2026, v2) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: Large test (26K real open-ended queries, 25 models) of within-model repetition and across-model similarity. Different models give strikingly similar answers, so cross-model pooling gives less variety than hoped. Aggressive decoding (min-p, temperature 2.0) barely reduced it.
numbers: Cross-model average pairwise similarity 71% to 82% (DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 vs gpt-4o 0.81). Within-model, top-p 0.9 and T=1.0: in 79% of cases average similarity exceeded 0.8. With min-p 0.1 and T=2.0, 81% of response pairs still exceeded 0.7 and 61.2% exceeded 0.8. 'Write a metaphor about time': 25 models x 50 samples fall in two clusters (river, weaver). Embeddings: text-embedding-3-small.
limits: Embedding similarity can overstate sameness for short texts; general queries, not blends. Authors lean to training-time fixes.
agent_relevance: Pooling providers is no guarantee of diversity (fits the KOMBINE 19.9% reuse figure). Diversity must come from the inputs (seeds, constraints).

source: Moon, Cho, Borrajo, Ganesh and Hashemi (2026) Breaking homogeneity: diversifying persona sets for creative LLM outputs
finding: Geometry-aware persona sets (space-filling selection or evolved personas) raise diversity far more than random personas. Random personas give a small gain. Gains hold on AUT, Infinity-Chat and DAT.
numbers: Generator Gemma-4-31B, judge Qwen3.6-27B, five seeds. AUT hull-extent diversity 1.42 (task-only) to 1.54 with RANDOM personas (+8.7%), originality +10.2%, creativity +8.9%; EVOLUTION personas 2.53 (+78.8% diversity), originality 13.61 (+26.1%), flexibility +49.5%, creativity +13.9%, validity 98.5%, utility drop 0.22 (-5.1%). Pool coverage 62.3% to 96.5% by MCMC. Correlation of pool geometry with response dispersion r=.40 (90% CI -.19 to .78) on AUT, r=.55 (CI .12 to .81) on a second set.
limits: Preprint, mid-size open models, diversity as embedding spread. Not blending. Cost of building the persona pool is not charged to the arms.
agent_relevance: Choose seeds to be spread out in embedding space (maximum distance among selected pairs), not drawn at random.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: LLM pools collapse under repeated sampling: from 4,000 seed ideas per topic only about 5% remained after de-duplication at cosine 0.8. Scaling samples at one prompt gives sharply diminishing unique ideas.
numbers: 4,000 generated seed ideas per topic, de-duplication threshold cosine 0.8, about 5% non-duplicated left; the human study used 79 reviewers from 32 institutions.
limits: NLP research ideas, not blends. Only the duplication result was checked here.
agent_relevance: Repeated sampling at one prompt wastes compute: de-duplicate, then spend tokens on varied inputs.

finding: Full text opened (Psychonomic Bulletin and Review 4:167-183). A theory paper: beyond relation linking, two more processes are needed, comparison and construction. Three interpretation types: relation linking, property mapping, hybrid. Hybrids get more frequent as the two nouns get more similar, which is the evidence for a comparison (alignment) process. Closes gap 7 for Wisniewski 1997.
numbers: Cites Wisniewski (1996a): among 3,003 meanings of 224 novel combinations from 189 subjects, 70% involved construing a noun's referent as something other than its typical category. Examples: zebra clam (property: clam with stripes, stripes rebuilt to fit a clam), zebra horse (hybrid, stripes placed along body and neck by alignment). Drill pamphlet cannot be a hybrid because the functions conflict.
quote: people align or put into correspondence the structure of the modifier and head concepts
limits: Mostly theory and review; the counts come from earlier experiments, not new ones. No LLM content.
agent_relevance: Comparison then construction maps onto a two-step blend operator: align the two seeds, name the key difference, rebuild that difference in the other concept's terms. Reject hybrids whose functions conflict.

source: Ye, Tu and Pustejovsky (2025) Enhanced noun-noun compound interpretation through textual enrichment
finding: Spelling out the hidden event that links head and modifier lifts LLM accuracy on noun-compound relation choice, most for weaker models. About 55% of benchmark compounds allow more than one reading. GPT-4o stays best.
numbers: Accuracy, baseline to enriched (three prompt settings per model, Rambelli et al. 2024 nine-way multiple choice). Lexicalised set: GPT-4o 69.6 to 74.4, 65.8 to 73.7, 65.0 to 70.8; Mistral first setting 59.1 to 70.8. Novel set, same head: GPT-4o 51.4 to 55.7, 52.0 to 57.8, 52.8 to 58.3. Novel set, same modifier: Mistral 30.1 to 34.2, 47.9 to 50.6, 30.5 to 51.3. Open models gained more than 9 points at compound level; GPT-4o less.
limits: Multiple-choice relation labels, not free generation. GPT-4o is 10-15 points lower on novel than on lexicalised compounds, which hints at memory support. No nonsense-word test.
agent_relevance: Even for GPT-4o, new combinations are harder than known ones, and an explicit 'state the linking event' step helps cheaply.

source: Ciapparelli, Zarbo and Marelli (2025) Conceptual combination in large language models: uncovering implicit relational interpretations in compound words (Cognitive Science)
finding: Abstract only (Wiley PDF blocked). With BERT-base and Llama-2-13b, swapping a compound for its paraphrase changes the embedding in inverse proportion to human plausibility ratings. This holds for existing and novel compounds, but is substantially weaker for novel ones, and older distributional models beat the LLMs there. Bears on gap 10 only for older models.
agent_relevance: Weaker novel-compound fit fits the idea of partial reliance on memory of real words.

source: Chen, Poeppel and Zuanazzi (2023) Meaning creation in novel noun-noun compounds: humans and language models
finding: Abstract only (OSF). Unconstrained interpretations of a large set of novel noun-noun compounds. Lexical features (material, agentivity, imageability, similarity) steer the grammatical relation. GPT-2, BERT and RoBERTa predict whether a compound is interpretable and its processing cost, but are blind to finer grammatical differences.
agent_relevance: Interpretability of a novel pair can be predicted from embeddings, a possible cheap pre-filter for seed pairs.

source: Absence check: gap 8 (modern large-sample replication of Hampton)
finding: Crossref title searches for overextension, guppy effect and emergent-attribute replications returned only Hampton 1988 and 1996 items, a 2005 logic paper and a 2017 plural-conjunction paper. No large-sample (N over 200) replication was found. This is absence of evidence from a tool-limited search, not proof.
limits: Web search quota was exhausted; arXiv search and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited. Only Crossref title search and some arXiv listing pages worked.
agent_relevance: Treat the human effect sizes as one-lab estimates when weighting design choices.

finding: No paper found that (1) adds an explicit generic-space step to LLM blending and measures valid-blend rate, (5) runs membership judgments for A, B and A-and-B in both orders on frontier LLMs, (6) tests Costello and Keane constraint filters with an LLM judge, (9) compares PopBlends-style pipelines with free blending at larger N, or (10) repeats the nonsense-word test on frontier models. Searches were limited, so these stay open rather than negative.
limits: Limited search tools (see d13). Repeat with a working web-search tool.
agent_relevance: Our own harness would be the first test; plan it as an experiment, not a citation.

finding: The paper argues a combination must create a new category that differs from the head category in a way tied to the modifier, and that noun meanings constrain sensible readings.
quote: It would be very implausible, for example, to interpret diamond oil as 'oil for lighting diamonds.'
limits: Theory statements, not tested on LLMs.
agent_relevance: The 'difference tied to the modifier' rule is a testable filter for the plausibility step in a blend scorer (partial stand-in for the unopened Costello and Keane 2000).

source: Ye et al. (2025) enrichment pipeline: polysemy and condition cues
finding: Compound meaning is often ambiguous, and giving the model a condition cue for each reading helps. The authors checked their automatic enrichment pipeline by hand.
numbers: About 55% of benchmark compounds admit more than one plausible reading. Pipeline: 90.3% agreement on binding; 84.4% pipeline accuracy; 15.6% of predicted relations needed manual revision; 25.7% of generated condition cues and 12.1% of context sentences needed regeneration.
limits: Data-curation numbers, not model results. Multiple choice only.
agent_relevance: Expect about one in four automatically generated 'condition cues' to be wrong; filter them.
